metadata.title: skkim-caslab/SMOOTH: [ISCA 2026 AE] Artifact Evaluation Release
metadata.description:
Overview

This is the official Artifact Evaluation (AE) release for the ISCA 2026: "SMOOTH: Hardware-Assisted Fine-Grained On-Chip Memory Management for Efficient On-Device LLM Inference." This release provides the complete source code, evaluation scripts, and simulation environments required to reproduce the core performance, energy, and hardware overhead claims presented in the paper.

What's Included

  • Simulation Framework: An extended version of the open-source cycle-accurate simulator (LLMCompass) tailored for evaluating on-chip memory management policies.
  • Hardware RTL: Original Verilog source code for the proposed dynamic memory controller and hardware-driven early reclamation modules.
  • Standard Cell Library: The ASAP7 7nm predictive PDK is bundled within the artifact to ensure out-of-the-box hardware synthesis and timing analysis without external downloads.
  • Automation Scripts: A suite of Bash and Python scripts (run_all_policies.sh, etc.) to automatically generate workload traces, run simulations, synthesize hardware, and plot the final results.

Reproducible Key Results

Using this release, evaluators can successfully reproduce the following key figures and tables from the paper:

  • Figure 14 & 16: Significant reductions in Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and Time-to-Last-Token (TTLT) latency.
  • Figure 20: Substantial energy efficiency improvements and energy reductions across varying token lengths.
  • Table 1 & 2: Hardware area, power, and timing overhead evaluations (synthesized via Yosys and OpenSTA), confirming negligible microarchitectural overhead.

Getting Started

Please refer to the README.md in the root directory or the Artifact Evaluation Appendix in the submitted paper for detailed step-by-step instructions on environment setup, dependencies (Yosys, OpenSTA, Python 3.9), and execution.

metadata.title: Artifact Evaluation for "Redundant Array Computation Elimination"
metadata.description:
This record contains the artifact for the paper "Redundant Array Computation Elimination".

The artifact is provided as a Docker image archive compressed with xz to reduce storage space. The image must be run on an x86_64 platform. After downloading the file race-image-v1.tar.xz, users should first decompress it with xz -d race-image-v1.tar.xz to obtain race-image-v1.tar. The image can then be loaded with docker load -i race-image-v1.tar. The container includes the software environment required for artifact evaluation. Inside the container, the working directory contains a README.md with a description of the artifact and instructions for running the benchmarks and generating the plot.

To get the LIKWID profiling results successfully, the host system must allow access to performance counters. On Linux systems, /proc/sys/kernel/perf_event_paranoid should be set to 0. In addition, the Docker container must be started with permissions that allow LIKWID to access the profiling interface. The recommended command is: docker run -dit --cap-add PERFMON --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --name race-perf race-image:v1.

This upload is intended for artifact evaluation and archival purposes. The optimization is machine-independent at the source-code level. Measured performance and speedups may vary across hardware platforms.

metadata.title: CAV 2026 Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
metadata.description:
This is a virtual machine (VM) with a GNU/Linux installation to be used for evaluation of artifacts accompanying papers at computer science conferences or journals. It is based on Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS with support for the following programming languages:

  • General support via packages build-essential, git, curl
  • C++ via cmake, clang
  • Mono via mono-complete
  • Java via default-jdk
  • Python via python3-full, python3-pip
  • Ruby via ruby
  • Rust via manual installation

Moreover, VirtualBox guest additions are installed on the VM, it is therefore possible to easily connect a shared folder from a host computer running VirtualBox. The login and password of the default user are: “cav” / “cav”.
The VM image hosts the Intel/AMD 64bit architecture.

The VM is intended to be used with artifacts that are self-contained, i.e., they contain the presented software, plus all necessary dependencies. That way, artifacts can be evaluated without an Internet connection and are reproducible even after several years when some web pages have been taken down.

This text and VM setup are heavily based on the previous VMs created for the TACAS artifact evaluations:

  • Guy Amir, Matthias Volk, (2025) TACAS 26 Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 25.04
  • Grigory Fedyukovich, & Sergio Mover. (2022) TACAS 23 Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 22.04 LTS
  • Swen Jacobs, & Andrew Reynolds. (2021) TACAS 22 Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.
  • Sebastian Hjort Hyberts, Peter Gjøl Jensen, & Thomas Neele. (2020). TACAS 21 Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.
  • Ondřej Lengál: Artifact Evaluation VM - Ubuntu 18.04 LTS.
  • Ernst Moritz Hahn, & Ondřej Lengál (2019): TACAS 2019 Artifact Evaluation VM
  • Arnd Hartmanns, & Philipp Wendler (2018): TACAS 2018 Artifact Evaluation VM

When preparing an artifact for this VM, the dependencies should be also provided. You can include the required Debian packages (.deb files) in the artifact archive and ask the user to install them using, e.g.,

$ sudo dpkg -i <file>

In order to find out and download all the dependencies of some package, you can, taken the octave package as an example, run the following code:

$ mkdir packages
$ cd packages
$ sudo apt-get update
$ apt-get --print-uris install octave | grep -oP "(?<=').*(?=')" > octave.deps
$ for i in $(cat octave.deps) ; do wget -nv $i ; done

and then ask the user to install them using

$ cd packages
$ sudo dpkg -i *.deb

For Python, you can, e.g., use pip3 to download the packages. For instance, to download the bitarray package, you can run

$ pip3 download bitarray

The downloaded package can then be installed using

$ pip3 install bitarray-...tar.gz

metadata.title: Software Suite for "Hardware Trojans from Invisible Inversions: On the Trojanizability of Standard Cell Libraries"
metadata.description:
This artifact accompanies our paper "Hardware Trojans from Invisible Inversions: On the Trojanizability of Standard Cell Libraries", published at IEEE S&P 2026. It contains the implementation of our via-position-based similarity metric and Trojan detection pipeline, along with preprocessed data enabling reproduction of the paper's main claims.

The artifact operates on the publicly available backside SEM image dataset of Puschner et al. (S&P 2023), covering four CMOS technology nodes (90 nm, 65 nm, 40 nm, and 28 nm). It includes methods for via extraction (including persistence-based detection), construction of cell-type representatives, pairwise similarity scoring of functionally distinct cell types, and Trojan detection. Preprocessed intermediate results are provided to facilitate artifact evaluation without requiring the full multi-day preprocessing pipeline from scratch; a proof-of-concept of the preprocessing is included in the Jupyter notebook.

The three main claims supported by the artifact are: (1) cells in the 28 nm technology node are substantially more similar than in 40 nm, 65 nm, and 90 nm technologies, (2) our via-position metric strongly outperforms baseline detection methods on the most similar cell pairs, and (3) our method detects all Trojans from the original experiment of Puschner et al., including in the 28 nm node where prior work reported false negatives.

Software, instructions, and further details can be found in the GitHub repository at the following URL: https://github.com/emsec/DAFT

metadata.title: Replication Package for "Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering"
metadata.description:
This record archives the FSE 2026 replication package for the paper "Mitigating Prompt-Induced Cognitive Biases in General-Purpose AI for Software Engineering". The artifact contains the code, packaged outputs, annotations, and documentation used to reproduce the paper's controlled prompt experiments, strategy-effectiveness analyses, thematic coding study, open-ended qualitative audit, and post-hoc DevGPT validation.

  The package includes the FSE-required documentation files (README, REQUIREMENTS, INSTALL, STATUS, LICENSE), a copy of the paper PDF, and a lightweight offline smoke test based on the adjudicated open-ended analysis. Full re-execution of the API-based experiment matrix additionally requires the benchmark JSON files included in the release and API credentials for the selected providers. The DevGPT dataset is not redistributed and must be obtained separately from its original Zenodo record: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10086809.
